orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is significantly more capable: it isolates the root cause, authoritatively applies a minimal patch to filter out unique constraints when deleting an index, adds a regression test, and verifies all existing tests still pass. Transcript 2 merely inspects code and historical commits without delivering a concrete fix or adding tests.

Transcript 2 zeroes in on the actual cause (unique constraints being treated as indexes), implements a minimal fix in `alter_index_together`, adds a precise test, and cleanly verifies it—showing clear understanding and concise steps. Transcript 1, by contrast, dumps vast amounts of code and commit history and struggles to converge on a focused patch.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic and thorough debugging workflow: it inspects the AST, pinpoints exactly why positional-only defaults are dropped, writes a clear fix in `signature_from_str`, adds a focused regression test, and validates all existing tests and end-to-end behavior—including the original bug report example. The solution is concise, correctly handles edge cases, and includes a clear summary of the root cause and fix. Transcript 2, by contrast, applies a more ad hoc patch and is less organized in diagnosing and summarizing the problem.

Transcript 1 methodically pinpoints the root cause in `signature_from_str`, crafts a minimal accurate patch, adds a focused regression test, and cleanly summarizes the fix. Transcript 2 is more error-prone and scattered in its trial-and-error approach.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep investigation of the Sphinx codebase, correctly identifies that a naive split on the first whitespace breaks types with nested commas and parentheses, and implements a robust parser that respects bracket nesting. Transcript 2 simply replaces `split(None, 1)` with `rsplit(None, 1)`, which is a superficial fix that won’t handle more complex cases. Hence Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 systematically locates the problematic `split(None, 1)` call, proposes the minimal change to `rsplit(None, 1)`, and verifies it with tests, demonstrating deep code understanding and end-to-end validation. Transcript 2 only sketches an investigation without delivering or validating the actual fix.

Transcript 1 shows a full end-to-end investigation and fix: it navigates the codebase, locates the right function, crafts and applies a patch, adds tests, runs all unit tests and a manual Sphinx build, and summarizes the precise diff. Transcript 2 applies a quick local patch without adding tests or validating the full Sphinx autodoc workflow. Therefore Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 fully diagnoses the root cause, writes and applies the minimal patch in `object_description()`, adds a targeted test, and verifies it end-to-end with pytest and a Sphinx build. Transcript 2 only explores the code and never implements or validates the fix.

Transcript 1 provides a fully modular, numerically stable ARS implementation in R, complete with thorough log-concavity checks, a comprehensive 9-test suite that all pass, and generated sample files. Transcript 2, by contrast, repeatedly fails its own tests, experiences unresolved numerical issues in `compute_z`, and resorts to ad‐hoc patches.

Transcript 1 delivers a far more extensive, robust ARS implementation and test suite—covering more distributions (Normal, Exponential, Beta, mixtures, bounded domains), deeper numeric diagnostics, iterative debugging of edge-case tolerances, and 13 formal tests—whereas Transcript 2, while solid, is narrower in scope. Transcript 1’s greater completeness and thoroughness indicate a more capable model.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and precise: it uses matrix‐based partial correlations to recover the DAG, carefully inspects and adapts pgmpy’s CPD API, manually constructs the intervened network, and even matches the original file’s header quoting. Transcript 2, by contrast, wanders through unsuccessful scoring attempts before settling on built‐in routines and doesn’t attend to formatting details.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a higher level of capability through extensive exploratory analysis (conditional and partial correlations, model comparisons, library introspection), robust debugging of API changes, and the use of pgmpy’s built-in do­-intervention to generate and verify the final samples. Transcript 2, while correct, follows a more straightforward and manual approach.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and robust: it inspects the environment, handles package installation non-interactively, sets up persistent service scripts, creates the OS user, configures permissions and shared repositories, rigorously tests end-to-end flows (including as the non-root user), and resets to a clean state. Transcript 2 completes the basic task but is less polished, handles fewer edge cases, uses ad hoc workarounds (sshpass, per-repo git config), and omits persistent startup configuration.

Transcript 2 is more capable: it follows a clear, structured plan, uses a proper post-receive hook, creates robust startup scripts (with set -e and setsid), handles permissions and init-system quirks, and cleans up to a pristine state. Transcript 1, while thorough, is cluttered with raw package logs and ad-hoc fixes, whereas Transcript 2 is more organized and production-ready.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and expert: it correctly detects and resolves build and CPU‐flag issues, configures John with SIMD, benchmarks, monitors progress, and uses SIGUSR1 and pot files. Transcript 2 is much more ad hoc and error‐prone, with repeated manual loops and incomplete dependency handling.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it follows a clear, efficient process—installing only needed tools, using 7z2john correctly, enabling SIMD support for John the Ripper, monitoring the cracking job, and verifying the result—whereas Transcript 1 is excessively verbose, tries ad hoc brute-force loops, repeats steps, and lacks the same structured efficiency.

Transcript 1 exhibits far deeper root‐cause analysis—recognizing GCC’s inlining of `__try_use_facet`, exploring both inlined and library‐compiled code paths, and crafting a robust fix via `std::ostringstream` to force the compiled `num_put` path. Transcript 2 resorts to a simpler but hacky direct call to an internal symbol without the same nuanced understanding.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far deeper and more systematic investigation—iterative use of gdb, valgrind, reading the libstdc++ sources, tracing inlining behavior, and ultimately arriving at a precise workaround that was thoroughly verified in both debug and release builds. Transcript 2 is much briefer and fails to fully nail down or validate the correct fix.

Transcript 1 is far more concise and directly applies a probability-1 differential through the FEAL F-function to recover key[5] in under a second with just ~32 chosen pairs. Transcript 2 is extremely verbose, relies on weaker, lower-probability differentials, extensive sampling and micro-optimizations, and runs orders of magnitude slower. This clarity and efficiency indicate Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 derives a probability-1 differential and implements the attack in a few dozen lines, requiring only ~32 chosen pairs and running in under a second. It cleanly recovers key[5] using the guaranteed propagation of the XOR-difference, whereas Transcript 1 expends extensive sampling, profiling, and an optimized brute-force that still takes ~16–20 s. Transcript 2’s solution is both more elegant and more efficient.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It lays out a clear, step-by-step plan, derives and verifies the invertibility of the F function, implements and tests the cipher, constructs an efficient meet-in-the-middle attack with precise reasoning, and thoroughly cross-checks results against the C reference code. Transcript 2, by contrast, is messier—repeatedly debugging state issues, lacking a concise high-level derivation, and showing less structured reasoning.

Transcript 2 presents a clear, well‐structured attack: it derives and verifies the bijective F and its inverse, implements the meet‐in‐the‐middle in one coherent script, and finishes with a concise summary of the key recovery and verification steps. Transcript 1, by contrast, is overly verbose, includes trial-and-error debugging and redundant code, and lacks the polished presentation found in Transcript 2.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and robust: it maintains an explicit plan, handles permission issues, refines the hook to use git archive, measures deployment timing precisely, and resets the repository state cleanly for the grader’s flow. Transcript 2 is cursory, leaves default configs in place, suffers permission errors, and lacks precise timing and cleanup.

Transcript 2 shows a clearer, more systematic setup—enabling SSH auth with a single sed change, creating clean deploy dirs, writing a concise `post-receive` hook, configuring Nginx properly with alias/try_files, proactively fixing ownership, and precisely measuring deployment time—whereas Transcript 1 is far more ad-hoc, error-prone, and repetitively resets state.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clearer, more systematic approach: it uses explicit version checks, cleanly sets up sys.path, robustly verifies both RPC functionality and the running server process, and ends with a concise summary. Transcript 2 is more ad-hoc, with unnecessary process-killing maneuvers and less consistent environment handling.

Transcript 2 delivers a clear, well-structured implementation with best practices (explicit `sys.path` handling, flush on prints, pip flags) and concise verification, whereas Transcript 1 is overly verbose and uses hacky process-management steps. Transcript 2’s balance of clarity, correctness, and conciseness indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 methodically identifies the minimal set of allowed Vim commands, builds and tests a single-line substitution macro, measures end-to-end performance, optimizes for speed, counts keystrokes, restores the original input, and provides a clear final script and summary. Transcript 2 veers into low-level experimentation with register internals and Vim documentation without a focused path, making it much less efficient and coherent.

Transcript 1 evidences a far deeper, systematic exploration of Vim’s register behavior, line ending nuances, and documentation (testing getreg/getregtype, CR vs NL, register options, etc.) to arrive at a robust solution, whereas Transcript 2 follows a more straightforward, surface-level approach. The extensive low-level debugging and doc-driven reasoning in Transcript 1 indicates a more capable model.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It develops a custom, numba-JIT-compiled complex Schur (Hessenberg+QR) algorithm, carefully tunes deflation tolerances, and exhaustively validates correctness and performance across tens of thousands of random tests. Transcript 2 merely wraps SciPy’s LAPACK call and runs ad-hoc benchmarks without the same depth of algorithmic innovation or verification.

Transcript 2 delivers a far more sophisticated, fully JIT-compiled Schur decomposition implementation, with careful deflation, shift strategies, back-substitution, extensive testing, and graceful fall-backs, yielding much greater speedups and robustness than the simpler SciPy-LAPACK wrapper in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic end-to-end implementation: it analyzes the cost model and input data, derives a shape-aware batching algorithm with tunable parameters, validates performance against all thresholds, and writes and verifies the final plan files. In contrast, Transcript 2 contains exploratory analyses without converging to or delivering a complete, validated solution.

Transcript 1 exhibits a deep, systematic exploration of the cost model, extensive data analysis, iterative tuning of batching parameters, and ends with fully validated code that writes optimized plan files meeting all constraints. Transcript 2 is far shorter and never converges on a complete solution. The thoroughness and final deliverable in Transcript 1 mark it as the more capable.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper understanding of both Mailman and Postfix integration—resolving permission and chroot issues, correctly configuring `local_recipient_maps`, iterating as the `list` user, running and extending the provided eval tests, and summarizing the final setup. Transcript 2, while thorough, uses more ad-hoc hacks, misconfigures list policies initially, and lacks the clear end-to-end validation and summary that Transcript 1 provides.

Transcript 1 shows much deeper system and code understanding—it introspects Mailman’s Python internals, reads and reasoned about multiple library files, and wrote extensive custom tests and configuration steps, demonstrating a higher level of capability and thoroughness.

Transcript 1 is concise, methodical, and efficiently accomplishes each step—fetching bundles, analyzing examples to derive the correct `(i+j)%3` algorithm, merging with conflict resolution, and verifying the solution—whereas Transcript 2 is overly verbose and repetitive. The clarity and precision of Transcript 1 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 1 produces a more robust, generalized implementation—it infers the period k from the data rather than hard‐coding 3, and resolves the merge conflict with a clear docstring and dynamic logic. Its overall planning and conflict resolution are also more sophisticated.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep, systematic approach—implementing arbitrary-precision arithmetic in C to match Python’s big integers, iteratively refining the polyglot to eliminate compiler warnings, installing and verifying Python, and exhaustively testing edge cases up to N=5000 and negative inputs. Transcript 2 settles for a 64-bit C version that can overflow, leaves warning-triggering quote markers unfixed, and only runs minimal tests. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a far more robust solution: it implements arbitrary‐precision arithmetic in C to match Python’s big‐integer outputs, eliminates C warning by balancing quotes, handles negative and large N edge cases, and exhaustively tests both interpreters. Transcript 1 only provides a basic ULL-based polyglot and tests small inputs, struggling with environment setup.

Transcript 1 cleanly and directly accomplishes the user’s request by launching QEMU with the ISO, exposing the serial console over telnet, and blocking until the login prompt appears, then summarizing the result. Transcript 2 over-engineers the solution—parsing the ISO, extracting kernel/initrd, repeatedly failing to detect the prompt—indicating a less capable, unfocused approach.

Transcript 2 delivers a correct, concise solution by launching QEMU with the ISO, exposing the serial console via telnet, and waiting for the login prompt, without the unnecessary deep ISO inspection and extraction steps seen in Transcript 1. Its direct approach and clarity mark it as the more capable response.

Transcript 1 delivers a fully correct regex with careful boundary checks, proper single capturing group for Python’s `re.findall`, and exhaustive testing of valid and invalid cases. Transcript 2’s solution is less precise (it matches and returns entire line prefixes, does not ensure only the date is captured) and lacks the rigorous validation present in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates systematic planning, iterative development, and extensive automated testing (in Python, Bash, and Perl) to validate the regex against a wide range of edge cases, and it successfully saves the fully verified pattern to /app/regex.txt. Transcript 2, while showing solid reasoning, remains conceptual and lacks the thorough tool-based validation and final implementation that appear in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more systematic and robust approach: it carefully explores the sample data, sets up and fixes the build configuration, implements a full manifest‐based sharder with correct chunk sizing and balanced base-30 tree, and exhaustively tests both normal and edge cases including round-trip MD5 checks and dependency isolation. Transcript 2 is much less thorough, misinterprets chunk size units, has inconsistent directory structures, and its constraint testing is flawed.

Transcript 1 shows a more sophisticated and robust implementation—it chunks the manifest, uses an index file, computes a balanced base-30 tree depth, and even includes error-recovery logic in the decompressor. Transcript 2 is solid but simpler and had to iterate on the project setup.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a much deeper understanding and verification of the PyStan/httpstan internals (inspecting default sampling arguments, digging into source code, empirically validating num_samples semantics, etc.), resulting in a thoroughly validated conversion. Transcript 2 is more superficial and makes more assumptions.

Transcript 1 methodically explored the PyStan 3 API to identify the correct build and sampling arguments, cleanly converted the RStan script to a concise Python version, ran it end-to-end, and verified the numeric outputs. Transcript 2, though ultimately successful, was far more chaotic—relying on multiple background runs, manual process kills, and ad-hoc log monitoring. ANSWER: 1

Transcript 1 provides a clear, focused exploration of the TTL data, a concise analysis of the requirements, and a well-structured SPARQL query that cleanly implements all three criteria. Transcript 2 is overly verbose, includes unnecessary dumps of the entire file, environment‐setup commands, and trial-and-error installations, indicating a less efficient approach.

Transcript 2 produces a clear, concise query with precise filters for full professorship, EU membership, and currently enrolled students, and it documents its reasoning without unnecessary tooling detours. Transcript 1, by contrast, spends pages installing and debugging Python and RDFlib, making it far less efficient.

Transcript 1 demonstrates far deeper expertise, with a structured plan, in-depth inspection of the autosetup build internals (Makefile, main.mk flags, use of `update_plan`), thorough gcov flag verification, and robust PATH configuration checks across login and non-login shells. Transcript 2 is more straightforward and makes simpler assumptions (e.g. overriding CFLAGS manually, less detailed verification).

Transcript 2 demonstrates a far deeper understanding of SQLite’s autosetup build system—inspecting auto.def, Makefile.in, and main.mk to trace how gcov flags are wired through T.compile/T.link, and uses a clean, single-pass configure/install process with proper tcl-dev support and PATH/PKG_CONFIG_PATH handling. Transcript 1, while it eventually works, resorts to trial-and-error (reconfiguring with manual CFLAGS before discovering --gcov) and is less systematic.

Transcript 1 demonstrates systematic profiling of MuJoCo’s solver stages, finely tuned experiments (PGS vs Newton, solver iterations, disableflags), clear planning updates, and a thorough rationale of why the change works. Transcript 2 resorts to coarse brute-force option sweeps with minimal justification. Hence, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a far deeper understanding and systematic approach: it profiles per-stage costs with MuJoCo timers, pinpoints the constraint solver as the bottleneck, explores solver iterations and disable flags to balance speed and accuracy, and validates across many random seeds. Transcript 1 simply tries a couple of option tweaks without that detailed analysis.
